transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Rafael (Redwood SE), Claire (Redwood Solutions), Liam (CTO), Priya (Head of ML), Evan (SRE), Nora (Product), Jonas (Infra)

Summary (auto): AuricStream is evaluating Redwood for their chat/streaming inference. Primary constraints are p95 latency for streaming responses, cost per 1k tokens, and VPC + KMS for data residency. They want to run a token/sec benchmark and compare Hosted vs Dedicated performance.

[00:00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros real fast, then we'll jump into your workload and the p95 targets you're trying to hit.
[00:00:18] Liam: Hey, Liam here — CTO at AuricStream. We build a live customer-support overlay that streams model responses back to users while they type. Our main ask is consistent p95 at scale, so — trying to understand the hosting path.
[00:00:35] Maya: Great. Rafael, want to kick us off on how Redwood typically approaches streaming p95?
[00:00:40] Rafael: Sure. So, at a high level we have three modes: Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private (VPC or on-prem). For streaming, the runtime optimizes KV cache, continuous batching where possible, and we do prefix caching when requests are similar. That said, streaming p95 depends on sequence lengths, token generation rate, and concurrency.
[00:01:05] Priya: To be explicit — our target is sub-300ms p95 for the first 1-2 tokens during streaming for 60 concurrent sessions, and sub-600ms p95 for steady-state token generation at ~40 tokens/sec per session. Is that realistic?
[00:01:24] Rafael: First 1–2 tokens at sub-300ms is a tough ask over hosted infra for larger models but doable with smaller optimized variants. For dedicated pools we can usually get better tail by controlling co-tenancy and kernel selection. We need to baseline with token/sec benchmarks though.
[00:01:45] Evan: Quick infra detail — our infra sits in us-east-1, VPC peering is possible. We require customer-managed KMS for keying request logs and SOC2 Type 2 compliance. How does Redwood handle that?
[00:02:02] Claire: We have Private deployments that offer a customer control plane with KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. For Hosted we offer encrypted-at-rest and we can integrate with external KMS for Dedicated through customer-managed enclaves — we can share the security deck.
[00:02:19] Nora: Cost is an important variable. If we go dedicated, what's the delta in cost per 1k tokens vs hosted? Ballpark is fine.
[00:02:30] Maya: We'll share a pricing sheet, but generally Dedicated has a base reserved capacity fee plus lower unit token costs. Hosted has zero reservation but higher per-token. We'll include concrete numbers in the followup.
[00:02:45] [timestamp jump — Rafael screenshare link referenced]
[00:02:50] Rafael: On this slide you can see a sample p95 breakdown — network ingress, model decode time, and post-processing. For streaming, there's extra latency from chunking and network flushes. Also worth noting: continuous batching can increase throughput but might add a few ms to median — though tail often improves because of better GPU utilization.
[00:03:17] Liam: When you say continuous batching improves tail, do you mean the p95 goes down, or the p95 variability drops?
[00:03:22] Rafael: Good question. In many workloads the variability drops and the p95 can improve because we avoid pathological single-token scheduling. But it depends on traffic mix. If you have a lot of single-token short responses, batching may add small queuing delay.
[00:03:40] Jonas: Our traffic is bursty — product launches lead to 3–5x traffic spikes for 15–40 minutes. Can Redwood autoscale quickly enough? We want to avoid cold-starts that blow p95.
[00:03:53] Rafael: Dedicated pools can reserve burst capacity; autoscaling policies can be tuned to pre-warm instances. We also offer model variants for faster cold starts and fallback policies to smaller quantized models to keep responses within SLOs.
[00:04:10] Priya: On quantization — we've seen 4-bit quantized models save cost but hurt quality. What's Redwood's stance on recommended quant profiles for streaming use cases?
[00:04:18] Rafael: We recommend mixed approach: FP16 or int8 for high-quality streams where latency matters. 4-bit is an option for background tasks but for customer-facing streaming we'd usually avoid heavy quantization unless you validate on your eval set. Redwood Optimize can give quantization recommendations based on prompt sets.
[00:04:40] [00:04:40] Liam: Ok, can we talk numbers: for a 2k token response at 40 tokens/sec and 60 concurrent sessions — what throughput and GPU count are we looking at in Dedicated?
[00:04:56] Rafael: Rough back-of-envelope. 2k tokens at 40 tokens/sec is ~50 seconds per session. At 60 concurrent sessions producing tokens simultaneously that's 2,400 tokens/sec sustained. If a single A100-like GPU can do say 8-12k tokens/sec depending on model and batch efficiency, you might be able to run that on a small pool — but streaming imposes additional overheads so plan conservatively. We'll run a benchmark to get exact tokens/sec for your model and prompt mix.
[00:05:28] Evan: That A100 number seems optimistic; our in-house results were 6k tokens/sec for our tuned model. We need Redwood's benchmark on our exact prompts.
[00:05:38] Rafael: Absolutely. We'll provide a harness that runs the sample prompts and reports p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. It will measure cold start, steady-state, and simulated traffic spikes.
[00:05:50] [00:05:50] Priya: On measuring p95 — do you include network latency from client device to API edge? We have users on mobile so RTTs vary.
[00:06:00] Rafael: Our internal p95 is measured server-side (model decode + server processing). For customer-facing SLOs you'd add your network RT as a budget: edge -> Redwood edge/cache -> GPU. For Hosted we have multi-region edges; for Private you'd host in-region.
[00:06:18] Nora: We also want token-level cost breakdowns in the console for billing ownership.
[00:06:23] Claire: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model. You can attribute cost to customers or teams.
[00:06:31] [00:06:31] Liam: Are there known failure modes for streaming? Like when the KV cache is missed or failing over models?
[00:06:39] Rafael: Yes — cache misses cause more memory and decode work; fallbacks to other variants can add a few hundred ms. We recommend prefix caching for common prompts and setting graceful fallback policies in the rollout: canary -> monitor -> full.
[00:06:55] Jonas: For Private, what does network topology look like? Is there a control plane that calls into our VPC? We need to ensure audit logs never leave our region.
[00:07:04] Claire: In Private mode we offer a customer-controlled plane. You can keep data and audit logs in-region, integrate with your KMS/HSM and have full ES/Splunk forwarding. We'll send architecture diagrams.
[00:07:18] Priya: Let's pin a concrete pilot scope. We want Redwood to run a benchmark on our top-10 prompts (avg seq len ~250 tokens, 2k max cases) and simulate our burst pattern (3x for 20 minutes). If we can see p95 numbers and recommended Dedicated pool size, we can move to a 2-week pilot.
[00:07:38] Rafael: That works. Ideal workflow: you share prompt set and traffic trace, we run hosted and dedicated runs with the harness, and produce a tech note with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec and recommended pool sizing and quant profiles.
[00:07:56] Liam: How long does that usually take? We're trying to align procurement timelines.
[00:08:01] Maya: Once we have your prompts and trace, benchmarks are typically 3-5 business days, then a short review session. Procurement can run in parallel; we'll include a draft SOW for Dedicated pilot.
[00:08:14] [00:08:14] Evan: Security checklist questions: SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs retention, data residency & deletion. Do you have an enterprise pack?
[00:08:24] Claire: Yes, enterprise pack covers SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC, extended audit retention, and SOC2/ISO attestation docs. We'll attach SOC2 report and a standard security questionnaire response.
[00:08:40] Priya: A micro question on batching: when a session is actively generating tokens, does Redwood batch across sessions or only across requests? We worry about per-session interleaving that affects ordering.
[00:08:53] Rafael: Streaming uses async emission with per-request tokenization; we may batch generate calls when it helps throughput but we ensure per-session ordering in the transport layer. We can tune the batch window to minimize interleaving for your use case.
[00:09:10] Maya: Quick commercial note — Dedicated often reduces per-token cost by 20–40% depending on commit. We'll put numbers in the sheet.
[00:09:18] [00:09:18] Jonas: Any gotchas with KV cache and long conversations? Our sessions average 14 turns with long context.
[00:09:26] Rafael: For long context we manage KV cache and chunking. For very long histories we might recommend truncated context + retrieval to keep latency low; Redwood Optimize can recommend caching windows for your workload.
[00:09:42] Priya: Ok, last technical: how do you handle model rollbacks if a deployment causes quality regression?
[00:09:48] Claire: Rollouts are canary by default with automatic rollback thresholds based on model-level evals and production metrics. We also support A/B traffic splits and automatic fallback to older variants.
[00:09:59] [00:09:59] Maya: Great — to recap next steps: (1) AuricStream shares prompts and traffic trace, (2) Rafael uploads benchmark harness and runs Host vs Dedicated runs, (3) Redwood shares pricing and security docs, (4) review session to decide pilot. Agreed?
[00:10:18] Liam: Agreed. One more small ask — can you include a short script that can run in our CI to reproduce the benchmarks?
[00:10:25] Rafael: Yes — we'll include a reproducible script and a small dockerized harness.
[00:10:30] [00:10:30] -- end of main discussion, Q&A --
[00:10:30] Nora: Are there examples of other customers with similar latency targets?
[00:10:36] Maya: We've worked with a few real-time chat vendors — some hit sub-200ms median for short sequences on Dedicated. We'll anonymize case studies.
[00:10:44] Priya: Any constraints on model size for Dedicated? We currently consider 13B and 70B variants.
[00:10:50] Rafael: Both are supported; 13B is usually much cheaper and faster. 70B will need more GPU memory and careful kernel selection. We'll run both if you want.
[00:11:05] Liam: For the pilot, if results look good, procurement will request a short Dedicated commit for a month. Will Redwood accept a short-term reserved capacity?
[00:11:14] Maya: Yes — we have flexible pilot commits for Dedicated.
[00:11:20] [00:11:20] Action recap (auto):
- Redwood: pricing sheet, security docs, benchmark harness
- AuricStream: prompt set and traffic trace
- Rafael: run benchmarks and produce sizing recommendation

[00:11:42] Evan: One small operational note — are logs available in real-time or batch? We prefer near-real-time streaming logs for metrics.
[00:11:51] Claire: We can stream logs to your customers' ingest (Kafka/CloudPubSub) or provide near-real-time dashboards in Console.
[00:11:58] Priya: Good. That covers my main concerns.
[00:12:03] Maya: Perfect — we'll follow up with the items in the next 48 hours. Thanks everyone.

[00:12:10] End meeting.

Transcript notes: informal speech, occasional filler, some mis-heard terms ("K-V cash" for KV cache), minor transcript artifacts where speaker labels are generic.
